gfx950 · CDNA4 · out‑of‑tree plugin

The LLIR Scheduler

An LLVM‑IR pass that keeps the matrix cores busy, by one of two models chosen per region: interleave MFMA with the LDS / global traffic that feeds it (a throughput ratio — §1–§7, typical of an intra‑wave GEMM hot loop), or fill each MFMA's co‑execution shadow with VALU and declare it with sched_group_barrier (co‑exec — §8–§9, typical of an inter‑wave Flash‑Attention DOT cluster, which is register‑only and has no memory latency to pair against).

The pass runs on LLVM IR (at the OptimizerLast extension point of the O3 pipeline, before codegen) and reorders the instructions of a GEMM hot loop so MFMA compute overlaps memory latency. To make that ordering survive codegen it pins each scheduled region with an llvm.amdgcn.sched.barrier rather than turning LLVM's machine schedulers off — so misched still runs everywhere else (§7). It ships as an out‑of‑tree LLVM pass plugin (libLlirSched.so) and is gfx950‑only: load it with LLVM_PASS_PLUGIN_PATH.

Scope. gfx950 (CDNA4) MFMA kernels — GEMM and Flash‑Attention. The pass identifies its eligible regions structurally, from what each region contains rather than from which kernel it came from (§8), and leaves everything else untouched — so it is safe to enable on any kernel: it simply does nothing on code that matches neither shape.

1 Pipeline — every block, transactional bail‑out

The same logic runs on every basic block of the function. There is no "find the loop" heuristic; a block that doesn't match the matrix‑core hot‑loop shape simply produces no schedulable regions and is left untouched.

For each basic block → Detect regions› Schedule regions

Each block is scheduled transactionally and independently: the pass snapshots the block, schedules it, runs verifyFunction, and—if that block's result is invalid—reverts only that block, leaving every other block's schedule intact. A failure in one block therefore does not throw away the work done on the others: the pass still reports success as long as at least one block was scheduled. A whole‑function clone‑and‑rollback wraps the entire pass as a backstop — it fires only in the rare case that the function is still invalid after the per‑block reverts, and only then does the whole kernel fall back to the default machine‑scheduled lowering.

It pins only what it schedules. The pass returns true if it scheduled at least one region, but nothing downstream depends on that signal: each scheduled region carries its own sched.barrier pins (§7). On a kernel where the pass finds nothing to do — or in a region it bails on — codegen is exactly the backend default, machine‑scheduled as usual.

3 Regions & the dependency invariant ★ key logic

The block is sliced into regions. The way a region is formed makes reordering within it dependency‑safe by construction — the scheduler can freely interleave a region's MFMAs with its memory anchors without consulting the def‑use graph.

Rule 1 — region boundary

Walking the block, a new region opens at each MFMA that follows ≥1 memory op (GR/LR/LW) since the current region began. A region is therefore one run of MFMAs followed by the memory ops that trail it, up to the next MFMA‑after‑memory. Consequence: within a region every memory op sits after all of that region's MFMAs. Memory ops that appear before a region's first MFMA belong to that region's setup and do not, on their own, open a new region.

Rule 2 — the dependency invariant

It follows from Rule 1 that an MFMA never consumes a load from its own region:

  • (a) Rule 1 ⇒ a region's loads come after all its MFMAs.
  • (b) SSA ⇒ an MFMA's operands are defined before it.

A load feeding an MFMA must precede that MFMA (b), which places it in an earlier region — never the MFMA's own region (a). So a region's MFMAs only ever read values produced outside that region (a loop‑carried PHI, or an earlier region's load), and the intra‑region interleaving in §5 can move MFMAs freely among that region's anchors without breaking any def‑use ordering.

Eligibility

A region is scheduled only when it contains both a recognized‑shape MFMA (§6) and at least one memory anchor to interleave against. Regions without an anchor, or whose MFMA shape isn't in the cost model, are left untouched — and a block whose regions are all ineligible contributes no scheduling at all.

Each is a minimal block; the right‑hand verdict is what the pass produces. These double as unit‑test cases.

When a region opens, the "seen a memory op" state is cleared, so a leading load (the region's own inputs) cannot split off the following MFMA. A boundary forms only on a memory op that appears after the region's MFMAs have begun.
Net: region formation alone makes intra‑region reordering dependency‑safe, and any block that isn't a matrix‑core hot loop yields no eligible regions — so the pass needs neither a loop‑finding heuristic nor a runtime prefetch check.

4 Per‑region pre‑processing

Two transforms prepare a region before its MFMAs are spaced out. Both exist only to keep the interleaving in §5 legal — neither reorders memory ops to hide latency.

TransformWhat movesWhere / why
Hoistshuffle/insertelement feeding an MFMA (same block)to the region start — unless it consumes a same‑region LR (that would break dominance)
Sinkextractelement defined by an MFMAto just after the region's last anchor
Why the sink is required, not cosmetic. Moving every MFMA‑result extractelement past the region's last anchor clears them out of the MFMA run, so the interleaving in §5 — which only reorders instructions before the last anchor — can never move an MFMA past one of its own result extracts.

5 MFMA interleaving budget ★ key algorithm

Anchors are processed in reverse and MFMAs are inserted after each. Every count is a throughput estimate — how much MFMA cover each memory op's issue‑port occupancy needs — never a latency‑hiding reorder. LDS accesses (reads and writes alike) pair at the exact cycle ratio; a global load takes a fixed 64 cycles of cover; the tail drains the run.

① MFMA ↔ LDS access (LR & LW) — a throughput ratio

An MFMA provides mfma_cycles of cover; an LDS access — a read (LR) or a write (LW) — occupies the one LDS issue port for a number of cycles proportional to its vector width (128 bits = 16 cycles). Reads and writes go through the same port, so the scheduler treats them identically: the pairing is simply the ratio of those two rates — cycles_per_access / mfma_cycles MFMAs per access. An access cheaper than one MFMA's cover shares an MFMA with its neighbours; a wide one draws several. The pass realizes this exactly by carrying a single running cycle balance across the region's LR and LW anchors:

cycles_per_access = LDS_bits / 8   (128‑bit access = 16 cyc)
balance   += cycles_per_access   // carried across the region's LR & LW
emit     = floor(balance / mfma_cycles);  balance −= emit · mfma_cycles

The width comes straight from the IR type — for a read the loaded vector (load <8 x half> / <4 x float> = 128‑bit, <4 x half> = 64‑bit, <16 x half> / <8 x i32> = 256‑bit), for a write the stored vector (store <4 x i32> to addrspace(3) = 128‑bit).

MFMA cyclesaccess widthcyc / accesspairing
16128‑bit161 MFMA : 1 access
32256‑bit321 MFMA : 1 access
1664‑bit81 MFMA : 2 accesses (= ½ cover)
32128‑bit161 MFMA : 2 accesses (= ½ cover)
16256‑bit (wide)322 MFMA : 1 access
matched (cost = cover)LRM two cheap accessesLRLWM wide accessLRMM

The pairing is the true throughput ratio over reads and writes together: two accesses each costing half an MFMA's cover share a single MFMA (1 MFMA : 2 accesses), while an access wider than one MFMA's cover draws more than one. The remainder of a partial pairing is carried to the next access, so no MFMA cover is lost across the region.

② GR & tail — the same throughput basis

A global load (GR) isn't an LDS access, but it's still costed by throughput, not latency: it occupies the global‑load path for a fixed ~64 cycles, so it needs 64 cycles of cover = ceil(64 / mfma_cycles) MFMAs.

MFMA cycle counts drive both the per‑GR budget and the per‑LR pairing. Scaled f8f6f4 shapes read cbsz/blgp to tell the input format apart.

mfma.scale.f32.32x32x64.f8f6f432 if both inputs f4 else 64 (either f8)

A 32‑cycle MFMA provides twice the cover per op, so it pairs with 2× the LDS accesses per MFMA and gets half the per‑GR count (2 instead of 4). A 16‑cycle MFMA is the 4‑per‑GR / 1‑per‑128‑bit‑access case.

7 Pinning the schedule with sched.barrier

For the interleave to reach assembly it has to survive LLVM's pre‑ and post‑RA machine schedulers. The pass holds its ordering by pinning each region locally, so misched keeps running everywhere else.

After a region is spaced out (§5), the pass drops an llvm.amdgcn.sched.barrier(0) immediately after each memory anchor in that region. A mask‑0 sched.barrier is a hard reorder barrier: misched may not move any instruction across it, so the exact MFMA↔memory ordering the pass chose is frozen — while the prologue, the epilogue, and any region the pass leaves unscheduled are still machine‑scheduled normally. The scheduler is never disabled globally, and nothing downstream (make_amdgcn) has to turn it off.

each anchor is pinnedGRMMMMsched.barrier(0) …so misched can't undo itLRMsched.barrier(0)
Self‑contained. Because it pins locally, the pass needs no companion change in the compiler to hold its schedule, so it loads as a plugin via LLVM_PASS_PLUGIN_PATH at the OptimizerLast extension point. (Its one compiler‑side requirement is unrelated to scheduling — LLVM_PASS_PLUGIN_KEEP_TARGET_MACHINE=1, so the O3 run keeps its target machine when a plugin is loaded.)

8 Region routing — which model ★ key logic

The choice is a property of what a region contains, not of which kernel it came from (WP::classifyRegion). It reuses the same classifySchedInst used in §2, so the two models can never disagree about what counts as memory.

Region containsModelWhat happens
MFMA + memory GR LR LW, no VALU throughput §5's cycle‑paired anchor walk. The intra‑wave GEMM case.
MFMA + VALU, no memory co‑exec §9. The inter‑wave FA case — TRITON_WP_DEBUG confirms those DOT clusters carry zero LDS effects, so there is no latency to pair against.
MFMA + VALU + memory not handled Skipped with a logged reason. An intra‑wave FA kernel would land here; the two models disagree about what an MFMA is for (covering VALU issue vs covering memory latency), so declining beats guessing.
no MFMA — Nothing to schedule around. FA's mem stages are this case; LLIRSCHED_WP_MEMNOP paces them separately with s_nop at the stage head.
Inter‑wave GEMM needs no scheduling at all and simply produces no qualifying region. Region boundaries for the co‑exec path come pre‑made: ConvertWarpPipeline lowers every warp‑pipeline stage boundary to llvm.amdgcn.sched.barrier(i32 0), so a region is the span between two of them.

9 Co‑exec model — sched_group_barrier ★ key algorithm

An MFMA occupies the matrix core for many cycles while the vector ALU sits idle beside it. Those two units issue independently, so VALU work placed behind an MFMA co‑executes with it and costs nothing — until the VALU exceeds what the MFMA covers, at which point the surplus is exposed and the matrix core waits. The model's whole job is to decide which VALU goes behind which MFMA.

The co‑execution window

An MFMA's window is shorter than its matrix occupancy: a 32×32×16 (32‑cycle) MFMA exposes 24 cycles of co‑execution. That is the budget each MFMA offers, and it is derived per region rather than assumed — regionWindowCycles reads the region's actual MFMAs via getMFMACycles (§6) and returns occupancy − 8, taking the shortest when shapes are mixed and bailing out entirely on an unmodelled one. Hardcoding 24 would over‑fill every window by 3× on an FA variant built from 16×16×32 MFMAs.

Not everything co‑executes. Transcendentals and packed math never issue alongside an MFMA (isNeverCoissue), which is why TRANS carries its own IGroupLP mask and packed ops cost two slots of window.

Cost model per op

Cycles a co‑issued op consumes from its window. Six plain VALU fill a 24‑cycle window.

OpCyclesNote
plain VALU4one co‑exec slot; a 24‑cycle window holds 6
packed v_pk_*8two slots' worth of window, but declared as one instruction — sched_group_barrier sizes are instruction counts
TRANS (v_exp)8own IGroupLP mask (0x400) — canAddMI's VALU branch excludes transcendentals
v_permlane20cross‑lane shuffle; one window hides a permlane plus a single 4‑cycle op
fneg, llvm.fabs0not instructions — they fold into the consumer as source modifiers

How the schedule is expressed

The pass does not reorder the region; it declares the intended pipeline as [MFMA 1][VALU n] / [MFMA 1][TRANS n] groups and lets AMDGPUIGroupLP build it in the machine scheduler. sched.barrier(0) pinning (§7) is only advisory by comparison — codegen still consolidated the last groups of a stage. Placement is not optional: IGroupLP forms groups scanning upward, so the whole declaration must sit after every real op of the region.

① The VALU fits the windows

Classify into dependency‑ordered blocks — VALU independent of the region's TRANS, then TRANS, then the VALU that consumes it — and pack each block into ceil(total/window) groups aimed at the average of what is left. Program order is too fine (FA's PV stage emits 8 alternating sub/exp runs, which do not fit 16 windows), and one flat VALU block is unsatisfiable whenever a VALU consumes a TRANS — IGroupLP abandons the pipeline and leaves ISel's order. Three blocks is a topological order of the class dependency, so it is always satisfiable.

This path imposes an order: VALU → TRANS → dependent VALU. Every TRANS‑independent VALU is declared ahead of the first TRANS, even where interleaving them would be equally legal. The order is always dependency‑safe, but it is a choice, and an empirical one — VALU‑first measured 2.3% faster than TRANS‑first on FMHA v3. A kernel whose natural order is TRANS‑first gets reordered accordingly. The over‑capacity path (②) makes the opposite choice: it emits in program order and never reorders classes, which is precisely what lets one window hold a VALU group and a TRANS group together.

② The VALU does not fit

fmha_v3 carries 476 and 496 cycles of VALU against 384 of capacity, so no arrangement hides it and the balanced packer merges cheap pairs into 48‑cycle groups. The question changes to which ops get a window and what shape the rest take (declareRegionGroupsOverCap; opt out with LLIRSCHED_WP_NOOVERCAP):

#RuleWhy
1Non‑splittable ops claim windows first — TRANS, the max3 reduction, v_cvt_pk, permlanePacking cannot help them, so they have first call on scarce capacity
2Remaining capacity buys packable ops from the end of the stage backwardsMFMAs inserted in reverse program order keep the uncovered remainder contiguous, where it already sits
3Covered packed ops are scalarized by the pass; uncovered ones stay packedA covered op should co‑issue 4 cycles at a time; an uncovered one is hidden by nothing either way, and one v_pk_mul_f32 retires two elements in one issue where two v_mul_f32 need two
4A window may hold groups of different classes[MFMA 1][VALU 1][TRANS 1] puts a sub and an exp2 behind one MFMA. fmha_v3's PV stage ends in exactly that pair and used to spend two windows on 12 cycles of work — worth +0.6%
Rule 3 means the pass does its own scalarization, on exactly the ops it decided to cover. A blanket split of every packed op in the region would defeat it — the uncovered ones must stay packed — so this path cannot be combined with one.
Where it stops. fmha_v3's PV cannot do better on packed coverage: 368 of its 384 cycles are unpackable, so only 16 cycles (2 v_pk_fma) can ever be bought while rule 1 holds. The 14 that stay packed are arithmetic, not a packing failure.

Knobs

None of these is needed for the measured configuration — the two that used to be are now defaults. With no LLIRSCHED_* set, the pass declares via sched_group_barrier and paces mem stages with 2 s_nop, which builds byte‑identical assembly to the old explicit recipe.

Env varEffect
LLIRSCHED_WP_NOSGBfall back to physically reordering + pinning (§7) instead of declaring (§9) — slower, kept for A/B
LLIRSCHED_WP_MEMNOP=koverride the mem‑stage pacing; default 2, 0 disables
LLIRSCHED_WP_NOOVERCAPkeep the fitting packer (①) even over capacity — for bisecting a regression to ②
LLIRSCHED_WP_DEBUGper‑region model, counts, group sizes and the chosen window
Everything else is hardwired to the measured winner. The heuristics that were once env‑selectable — counting the max/min reduction, the 2:1 v_maximum3 fold, adaptive group weight, pinning the physical interleave, the legacy error‑diffusion spread, pre‑reordering before a declaration — each had a losing alternative, so the loser is gone rather than left as a flag.
Safety. The whole pass is transactional — clone the function, schedule, run verifyFunction, and roll back to the pristine body on failure — so a bad schedule can never reach codegen. It earned its keep: a phi‑led region once rolled back an entire interleave, costing 8%, until the region walk learned to advance past phis.
